then.text: Off to the SS Great Britain next, is it? Down at the harbour, in the very dock she was built in. Give her my regards.

else.text: Brunel's notebook! Well I never. Page one: 'Clifton. Span: 702 feet.' That's 214 metres, give or take.
He was only 24 when he won it. He called the bridge 'my first child, my darling'. His words, not mine.
There. I've put the toll booth's stamp on the page. Next stop, the ship.
The deck's 214 metres from tower to tower. Folk on foot pay nothing; cars pay a toll, as they have since 1864.
Brunel wanted sphinxes on top of the towers. Egyptian style was all the rage. The money ran out. The towers are still waiting.

then.text: There she goes! Up over the gorge on the evening breeze. You can see right down the Avon to the Severn from up there.
Fiesta's in August, but between you and me, the best flights are any still morning with a flask.
Burner on... a long roar... and she's filling! Look at her stand up! Crew, hands on the basket!
We're off! Light as a feather. Wave to Clifton! Wave to the goats!
Down we come in a field by the orchard, gentle as you like. Champagne for the farmer: an old balloonists' custom.
You've earned this. A little wicker sprite has been living in my spare basket all summer. It likes you. Take it.

else.text: Envelope? Got it. Burner? Got it. Now I need a ground crew, and the best one in Bristol hangs about the Harbourside.
Their crew chief only takes orders from someone who's beaten her. Off you go!
Lovely envelope! Next, my burner's valve is shot. The engineers at Aerospace Bristol, out at Filton, owe me one. Ask for a spare.
Still waiting on my envelope from the Balloon Works in Bristol. South of the harbour, by the Sanctuary.
Oh, thank goodness, a pair of hands! I'm Gwen. I fly balloons. Well, I fly them when they're not in bits.
Hot air's lighter than cold air, so you heat the air in the envelope and up you go. It's been working since 1783.
But my envelope's torn, my burner's sulking and my crew have gone to the pub. Can you help me get airborne?
Help Gwen get airborne?

then.text: Brilliant! First, the Balloon Works in Bristol are patching my envelope. Fetch it for me?

else.text: Fair enough. I'll be here, staring at the sky.

then.text: The tiercel brought her a pigeon this morning, mid-air. Passed it claw to claw. Romance isn't dead.
That's a peregrine! Look at that moustache stripe, those yellow feet. Beautiful. Thank you for showing me.
Here, take this. A moulted feather from the ledge, found fair and square. It's said to make a creature quick off the mark.
That's a peregrine! Look at that moustache stripe, those yellow feet. Beautiful. Thank you for showing me.
Here, take this. A moulted feather from the ledge, found fair and square. It's said to make a creature quick off the mark.

else.text: Last task: catch a peregrine yourself. They hunt over the gorge at dawn and by day. Bring one to show me.
Ask the pigeon fancier on the Downs what peregrines eat. He'll have opinions. Loud ones.

then.text: Here, have a look through the scope. Left of the bridge, two-thirds down the cliff. See the ledge with the white splashes?
There she is! The falcon. The female's bigger than the male, by about a third. The male's called a tiercel, from the Latin for a third.
They've raised chicks here most springs. Some years we get three or four. Now, a bit of homework for you.

else.text: Peregrine watch! Every spring we set up the scopes here so anybody can see the falcons on the cliff.
They were nearly wiped out in the 1960s by pesticides that made their eggshells thin. They've come back. Want to help with today's watch?
Join the peregrine watch?

then.text: Here, have a look through the scope. Left of the bridge, two-thirds down the cliff. See the ledge with the white splashes?
There she is! The falcon. The female's bigger than the male, by about a third. The male's called a tiercel, from the Latin for a third.
They've raised chicks here most springs. Some years we get three or four. Now, a bit of homework for you.

else.text: The falcons aren't going anywhere. Well, they are, at 300 kilometres an hour, but they'll come back.

then.text: Still here. Still counting my birds. Still one short.

else.text: What do peregrines eat? Pigeons! My pigeons! Racing pigeons worth more than my car!
Well, pigeons mostly, and starlings, and the odd duck. They catch them in the air, in a dive. Clean as you like.
Townie pigeons, mind, are why falcons do so well in cities. Cliffs, cathedrals, tower blocks: it's all ledges to a peregrine.
Alright my lover. Racing pigeons, me. They can find their way home from France. I can't find my way home from the pub.

gorge_goatherd.text: Those goats are feral, from a herd brought in to graze the cliffs. They nibble the scrub off the rocks so the little rare plants get the light.
Best workers we've got. No breaks, no complaints, and they do the bits a person would need a rope for.

orchard_farmer.text: Proper West Country cider's just apples, pressed and left to get on with it. Kingston Black, Yarlington Mill, Dabinett. Lovely names, lovely trees.
Scrumpy's the rough stuff, cloudy, from the farm. It's like a pasty: there's a right way, and there's the way the tourists have it.

leigh_forager.text: Leigh Woods belongs to the National Trust now. It was given to the nation in 1909 so Bristol could never build over it.
In autumn the woods fill with fungi. Look, don't pick. That one there could have you, and it knows it.
